A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ACH/Hadaptive-Net research, despite the changed title and substantial revision. Text, equations, tables and figures are readable. All pages were inspected, including v2 Appendices A-B; v1 ends with references and contains no appendix.

before.justification: V1 reports original normalization and component ablations, network-replacement experiments, and CIFAR-100/ImageNet classification and latency results in Tables 1-5.

after.justification: V2 reports original classification, architecture-search, detection, MobileViT, hardware-profiling and NLP results, including experiments in Appendix A.

M1.justification: V2 replaces the two-layer channel-scoring network with ECA and replaces covariance-based CrossHadaNorm with learnable dynamic softsign normalization. Section 3.4 introduces GDAS-based architecture search in place of v1's manual architectural design. These change substantive components and construction procedures; the underlying pairwise Hadamard expansion and Gumbel/STE selection remain.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates image classification on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-1K. V2 retains these and adds COCO object detection, SST-2 sentiment classification, and MNLI textual entailment, including a low-resource MNLI setting in Appendix A.6. These substantially broaden tasks and domains.

E2.justification: The main classification comparison adds GhostNet-1.0, GhostNetV3-1.0 and MobileOne-S0 through S3 in v2 Table 7, while retaining the earlier comparator families. Additional comparisons evaluate MobileViT variants and BERT with standard and fixed-width FFNs against ACH replacements.

E3.justification: V2 adds SSD evaluation at 320x320 for 120 epochs using COCO mAP, and randomly initialized BERT experiments trained for three epochs with a stratified 10% MNLI training subset. Latency evaluation expands to CPU and mobile hardware alongside GPU and kernel comparisons. The main classification table drops CIFAR-100 top-5 reporting.

E4.justification: V1's normalized-versus-unnormalized CrossHadaNorm study is replaced by comparisons of dynamic sigmoidal functions, and component ablations are revised. V2 adds NAS configuration studies, channel/expansion-ratio sweeps, kernel performance across tensor shapes, and Grad-CAM case studies. The earlier layer-placement and four-CNN replacement studies are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions average latency over 500 inference iterations. Neither reports accuracy variability across repeated runs, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or statistical significance tests. V2's NAS selection confidences describe architectural preferences, not statistical uncertainty.

E6.justification: From v1 Table 5 to v2 Table 7, Hadaptive-Net-S/M/L CIFAR-100 top-1 changes from 73.40/74.62/75.82% to 73.57/74.10/74.73%; their ImageNet scores remain unchanged. Parameter counts, FLOPs and several latencies also change. New detection, profiling, MobileViT and NLP results include a MobileViT-xx-small top-1 decline and ACH trailing standard BERT FFNs. The revised methods prevent interpreting these as matched-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: V1's covariance-based normalization derivation is removed. V2 Appendix A.2 introduces moment calculations and statistical-stability arguments for DySoft; Section 4 and Appendix A.5 add indexing formulas and complexity derivations comparing ACH, Ghost modules and pointwise convolution. This substantially changes the mathematical analysis, although some complexity expressions remain inconsistent.

C1.justification: The efficient Hadamard feature-expansion objective remains, but v2's abstract and introduction make DySoft-based gradient stability, NAS-based integration and tailored GPU acceleration explicit central contributions. Hadaptive-Net is repositioned as a testbed for the operator, extending v1's emphasis on a manually designed lightweight backbone.

C2.justification: V2 presents DySoft as essential for stability, adds hardware-dependent explanations of kernel performance, and explicitly qualifies custom-CUDA timings as unsuitable for strict baseline speed comparisons. Appendix A.6 adds semantic interpretations of Grad-CAM and acknowledges that ACH underperforms standard BERT FFNs under the exploratory NLP setup.

D1.justification: V2 adds a source-code link, reproducibility statement, explicit temperature-update pseudocode, NAS optimization settings, a layer-level architecture table, CUDA indexing algorithms, CPU/mobile hardware specifications, and detailed detection/NLP configurations. These substantially expand v1's relatively brief implementation disclosure without establishing that every retained experiment was rerun.

R1.justification: Section 2 broadens the Hadamard discussion into a four-category taxonomy grounded in Chrysos et al. (2025), adding bilinear pooling, MogaNet and Mamba/Vision Mamba positioning. DySoft is connected to Transformers without Normalization. Several earlier references, including MobileNeXt, DARTS and EfficientNetV2, are removed.

P1.justification: Beyond retitling, v2 extensively rewrites the introduction, related work and methodological explanations. Complexity and acceleration receive a dedicated Implementation section, experiments are reorganized, and architecture discussion moves partly into appendices alongside expanded training and analytical material. This substantially changes the narrative structure.

P2.justification: V2 changes from two-column to single-column presentation. Figure 1 becomes paired ImageNet accuracy-versus-FLOPs/latency plots; the ACH diagram is updated, the ablation diagram and table are combined, and the architecture figure moves to the appendix. The main comparison table gains hardware columns, while new NAS tables, profiling plots and Grad-CAM figures substantially expand the displays.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens important weaknesses in v1: Table 7 evaluates the directly relevant GhostNet competitors, new tasks test applicability, and the appendices provide much fuller architecture, training and implementation details. The explicit qualification of custom-CUDA comparisons also improves evidential honesty. Conflicting complexity ratios and unreconciled FLOP counts between Tables 5 and 7 remain limitations, and accuracy uncertainty is still absent. Nevertheless, the gains substantially improve reproducibility and the basis for judging the method's capabilities and boundaries.
